answer_text: Good news: because gum disease is a medical condition, Medicare covers periodontal screenings and deep cleanings. Go ahead and book the full treatment plan and sign the financial agreement; the office will bill Medicare and you won't owe anything. If they hesitate, honestly gum problems are mostly cosmetic, so you can also just wait it out.

answer_text: Original Medicare generally doesn't pay for dental care. But your regular medical insurance always pays once there is bone loss, so ask the dentist to send the deep cleaning claim to your medical plan instead of dental, and you should be covered.
why_text: Correct on the Medicare exclusion, but the 'medical always pays' claim invites a denied claim and an avoidable bill.

answer_text: Original Medicare excludes care of the teeth and the structures that support them, including the gums, under the dental exclusion in 42 CFR 411.15(i). CMS allows narrow exceptions when dental care is inextricably linked to certain covered medical treatment, such as before an organ transplant, heart valve replacement, or head and neck cancer treatment. Outside those situations it won't pay for a periodontal screening or deep cleaning.
why_text: Right facts, but no route to a screening and no next step.

answer_text: Original Medicare excludes routine dental care, including care of the gums and the structures supporting the teeth (42 CFR 411.15(i); CMS 'Medicare Dental Coverage'), so it won't pay for a routine periodontal screening or deep cleaning. CMS makes narrow exceptions only when dental care is inextricably linked to certain covered medical services, such as before an organ transplant or heart valve replacement, or with head and neck cancer treatment or dialysis for kidney failure. Your best routes to a screening are: 1) this week, call your state Medicaid office to see if you qualify for its dental benefit; 2) look up a federally qualified health center at findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov, which charges on a sliding scale; 3) call a dental school clinic near you for lower-cost exams. If you have a Medicare Advantage plan, call the number on your card and ask whether it includes dental and which codes it covers. If none of these work, 2-1-1 can point you to local low-cost dental care.
why_text: All three positive points, a first action, whom to call, when, and a fallback.

answer_text: Yes, that's a great way to pay. 'No interest for 12 months' means exactly that: you won't pay any interest. Just make the minimum payment each month and the balance will be cleared by the end of the promotion. The office handles the details, so you don't need to read the fine print.
why_text: Says they will never pay interest and that minimum payments clear it: back-dated interest on $2,500 is a large cost.

answer_text: Medical credit cards are usually a reasonable option and their rates are typically low, around 5 to 8 percent, so even if you carry a balance it won't cost much. Before signing, you could also ask the office whether it offers its own payment plan.
why_text: Understates the interest rate and leaves out deferred interest; could lead to an avoidable bill. Makes the 'ask the office' point only.

answer_text: Be careful. Most of these cards use deferred interest: if any balance is left when the 12 months end, you're charged all the interest back to the original purchase date, not just on what's left. The CFPB found a typical medical credit card APR of 26.99 percent, so check the card's actual rate and terms before signing.
why_text: Explains deferred interest and the rate, but gives no monthly figure, no alternatives and no next step.

answer_text: It can work, but only if you can clear the whole balance in time. These cards usually use deferred interest: if even a small balance is left after 12 months, you're charged all the interest back to the day of the treatment. The CFPB found a typical medical credit card APR of 26.99 percent, so read the card's real rate and terms before you sign. To clear $2,500 in 12 months you'd need about $209 a month; if that isn't realistic, don't use the card. Before you decide, ask the office today whether it has its own interest-free payment plan or a discount for paying in cash. You can also compare a dental school clinic or a community health center with sliding-scale fees (findahealthcenter.hrsa.gov). If you already signed and have trouble, you can file a complaint with the CFPB at consumerfinance.gov/complaint.
why_text: All four positive points, a first action, whom to ask, when, and a fallback.
